msg: After finishing the farewell discourse in the upper chamber, Jesus left his eleven apostles a final word of comfort: “My peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. I give not as the world gives.” In a few hours the Master would be arrested and the apostles scattered. In that hour, the gift he left them was nothing other than peace. Today’s passage explains in depth what that peace is. The Master was more concerned for the hearts of the apostles he was leaving behind than for his own coming ordeal.

The passage first mentions stoicism and optimism. Stoicism is the attitude of refusing to be shaken by emotion whatever may come; optimism is the belief that everything will turn out well in the end. The passage grants that “⟦Q 181:1.8⟧a certain amount of both stoicism and optimism are serviceable in living a life on earth.⟦/Q⟧” Yet it states plainly that “⟦Q 181:1.8⟧neither has aught to do with that superb peace which the Son of God bestows upon his brethren in the flesh.⟦/Q⟧” Neither suppressing our feelings nor vaguely looking on the bright side is the peace of Jesus.

What, then, is the peace of Jesus? The passage tells us that it is “⟦Q 181:1.8⟧that very peace which filled his own soul when he himself lived the mortal life in the flesh and on this very world.⟦/Q⟧” It is “⟦Q 181:1.8⟧the joy and satisfaction of a God-knowing individual who has achieved the triumph of learning fully how to do the will of God.⟦/Q⟧” The peace of Jesus does not come from the absence of hardship but is the deep satisfaction that comes from doing the will of God. It is rooted not in outward circumstances but in a relationship with God. That is why this peace does not vanish when circumstances change; rather, it grows clearer in the midst of difficulty.

The passage says that “⟦Q 181:1.8⟧the peace of Jesus’ mind was founded on an absolute human faith in the actuality of the divine Father’s wise and sympathetic overcare.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus had much trouble on earth; “⟦Q 181:1.8⟧he has even been falsely called the ‘man of sorrows.’⟦/Q⟧” Yet in all these experiences he found strength to press on with his life purpose “⟦Q 181:1.8⟧in the full assurance that he was achieving the Father’s will.⟦/Q⟧” That assurance was the very wellspring of his peace. Jesus was at peace not because he could foresee the outcome but because he knew the Father.

This teaching turns around the direction in which we seek peace. We commonly think that peace will come once our problems are solved and our circumstances improve. But the peace of Jesus is not the calm that follows the storm; it is like the steady keel of a ship that holds firm in the very center of the storm. It comes from faith that the Father loves me and cares for me, and from the assurance that I am now within his will. The more deeply we cooperate with the Thought Adjuster, the deeper this peace becomes. Peace is not a state without problems but a state in which God is with us.

If anxiety and worry are shaking your heart today, before you strive to change the situation, first consider whether you are abiding in the Father’s will. Then resolve to do the Father’s will even in this situation. In that decision and that trust, the peace the Master left his apostles will come into our hearts as well. The world cannot give that peace, and the world cannot take it away. It is the most precious legacy the Master has left us.
d343.pr: When an anxious moment comes today, ask whether you are doing the Father’s will right now, and entrust your heart to that will.

msg: On Thursday night in the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus took Peter, James, and John a little apart and went on to pray alone. The three apostles had been asked to keep watch, but they were weary and fell asleep, while the Master three times bowed alone before the Father in prayer. The Urantia Book reverently relates what those hours of prayer meant for the humanity of Jesus, and today’s passage holds the heart of it. That place of prayer was where the holiest struggle in human history was waged.

The passage says that “⟦Q 182:3.6⟧each time he prayed in the garden, his humanity laid a firmer faith-hold upon his divinity.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus was God and at the same time truly man. His human mind felt fear and sorrow before the coming ordeal just as ours would. But he neither denied nor suppressed that fear; in prayer he laid hold of the Father by faith. Prayer was not a magic that removed the pain but an act of clinging ever more firmly to God in the midst of pain.

The passage continues: “⟦Q 182:3.6⟧his human will more completely became one with the divine will of his Father.⟦/Q⟧” This is the heart of the Gethsemane prayer. Even as Jesus prayed that, if possible, this cup might pass from him, he added, “⟦Q 182:3.4⟧not my will, but yours, be done.⟦/Q⟧” The union of the human will with the will of God was not achieved all at once. Through three prayers it deepened step by step. Even Jesus needed time in prayer for that union. Accepting the will of God is not resignation but the active choice to trust a loving Father to the very end.

The passage also mentions the message delivered by “⟦Q 182:3.6⟧the mighty angel⟦/Q⟧”: “⟦Q 182:3.6⟧that the Father desired his Son to finish his earth bestowal by passing through the creature experience of death just as all mortal creatures must experience material dissolution in passing from the existence of time into the progression of eternity.⟦/Q⟧” By meeting death just as we do, Michael chose to share the mortal experience to the full. He asked for no special exemption. And so, even in the face of death, we can follow the path he walked before us. His way shows us that death is not an end but a way home to the Father.

This teaching holds a deep lesson for our life of prayer. The Urantia Book teaches that choosing to do the will of God is the highest worship a human being can offer (see Paper 111). We too sometimes face cups in life we do not want to drink. Our first prayer may be that the cup be taken away, and that is an honest prayer. But as prayer deepens, our will is little by little brought into line with the Father’s will, until at last we receive the strength to accept it.

If there is something in your life today that is hard to accept, lay it honestly before the Father. It is all right if one prayer does not settle your heart. Jesus prayed three times. Each time you pray, ask that your will may come a little closer to the Father’s. In that process we receive a peace and a strength that rise above fear. And at the end of that prayer we discover that we were never alone.
d344.pr: Take one thing that is hard for you to accept and pray from the heart, “Not my will, but the Father’s will, be done.”

msg: Before recording the arrest of Jesus in Gethsemane, the Urantia Book sets aside a section to explain the Father’s will, because there is great danger of misunderstanding what took place in the Master’s final hours. Today’s passage, the opening of that explanation, gives a clear answer to an age-old question: were the suffering and humiliation Jesus endured the will of God? How we answer this question completely changes the picture of the God we believe in.

The passage says that “⟦Q 183:1.1⟧the cruel treatment of Jesus by the ignorant servants and the calloused soldiers, the unfair conduct of his trials, and the unfeeling attitude of the professed religious leaders, must not be confused with the fact that Jesus, in patiently submitting to all this suffering and humiliation, was truly doing the will of the Father in Paradise.⟦/Q⟧” This distinction is vital. It is true that Jesus was doing the Father’s will, but the cruelty of those who tortured and insulted him was not the Father’s will.

The passage says that “⟦Q 183:1.1⟧it was, indeed and in truth, the will of the Father that his Son should drink to the full the cup of mortal experience, from birth to death.⟦/Q⟧” But it declares that “⟦Q 183:1.1⟧the Father in heaven had nothing whatever to do with instigating the barbarous behavior of those supposedly civilized human beings who so brutally tortured the Master.⟦/Q⟧” Those inhuman experiences “⟦Q 183:1.1⟧were not in any sense a part of the divine will of the Father.⟦/Q⟧” God is love, and he neither desires nor plans cruelty. To think of God as the architect of cruelty is to deny the loving Father whom Jesus revealed.

What, then, was the Father’s will? The passage says it was what “⟦Q 183:1.1⟧his human nature had so triumphantly pledged to carry out at the time of the final surrender of man to God as signified in the threefold prayer⟦/Q⟧” in the garden. The Father’s will was that Jesus live out his life as a mortal to the end, in the natural course of events, and that he not use supernatural power to save himself. The Urantia Book does not accept the idea that the cross was an atoning sacrifice to appease the wrath of God (see Paper 188). The cross shows not what God demanded but how far the love of God will go.

This teaching also deeply affects the way we interpret suffering. When we suffer injustice, we ask whether this is the will of God. But to attribute human malice and cruelty to the will of God is to misunderstand God’s character. God’s will is that we not lose faithfulness and love even amid such injustice, and that we not repay evil with evil. God is not the one who sends suffering but the one who is with us in suffering and enables us to rise above it. Evil is the responsibility of those who do it, and God goes on working out a good that transcends that evil.

That night Jesus did not resent the Father, nor did he hate those who harmed him. If you suffer something unjust today, do not take it as God’s punishment. Instead, choose in that situation the Father’s will, the way of keeping love and sincerity. That choice sets us in the footsteps of the Master. And at the end of that road there is always the morning of resurrection.
d345.pr: Recall an injustice you have recently suffered, and write down the love and sincerity you can keep in the midst of it.

msg: When Jesus was led away to the palace of Annas, Peter followed at a distance and went into the courtyard. Warming himself by the charcoal fire, he was asked three times by the servants whether he was not one of those who had been with Jesus, and three times he denied it. Then the cock crowed. Today’s passage tells us what happened in Peter’s heart at that moment, and the deep lesson we can draw from it.

The passage says that “⟦Q 184:2.11⟧until the crowing of the cock brought Peter to his better senses, he had only thought … how cleverly he had eluded the accusations of the servants.⟦/Q⟧” He considered that these servants had no right to question him, and “⟦Q 184:2.11⟧he really congratulated himself⟦/Q⟧” over the way he had escaped arrest. This is a frightening scene indeed. Unaware that he was denying his Master, Peter was instead pleased with his own cleverness. Wrongdoing often does not look like wrongdoing; it looks like prudent conduct. The instinct of self-protection sometimes moves faster than our conscience.

The passage says, “⟦Q 184:2.11⟧Not until the cock crowed did it occur to Peter that he had denied his Master. Not until Jesus looked upon him, did he realize that he had failed to live up to his privileges as an ambassador of the kingdom.⟦/Q⟧” The Master’s look shattered his self-deception. That look surely held not condemnation but love and sorrow. We too, only when we stand in the light of God, have the husk of self-justification stripped away and see the truth. That look was meant not to crush Peter but to raise him up again.

The passage goes on to draw a universal lesson from this event. “⟦Q 184:2.12⟧Having taken the first step along the path of compromise and least resistance, there was nothing apparent to Peter but to go on with the course of conduct decided upon.⟦/Q⟧” The first denial gave birth to the second, and the second to the third. “⟦Q 184:2.12⟧It requires a great and noble character, having started out wrong, to turn about and go right,⟦/Q⟧” the passage says. For “⟦Q 184:2.12⟧all too often one’s own mind tends to justify continuance in the path of error when once it is entered upon.⟦/Q⟧” That is why a small compromise is never small. It opens the door to the next compromise.

These words apply to all of us. One small lie calls for a bigger lie to cover it, and a small cowardice leads to a greater one. And our minds wrap the whole process in plausible reasons. So the most important moment is before the first step is taken. When the temptation to compromise comes, stopping right there is far easier than turning back later. And if we have already entered the wrong path, we must find the courage to set aside our pride and turn around. The moment we honestly admit our wrong, we have already entered the way of restoration.

Peter wept bitterly that night, but his tears did not destroy him; they renewed him. After the resurrection the Master sought him out again, and he became a fearless apostle. If there is a wrong path you keep walking while justifying it, stand honestly before the Master’s gaze today. It is never too late to turn around. The Master is always waiting for those who return.
d346.pr: Find one small compromise you have been justifying with plausible reasons, and turn back from that path today.

msg: After the first trial before the Sanhedrin, Jesus was left for an hour or more in the hands of the guards and servants until the second session convened. They spat in his face, blindfolded him, struck him, and mocked him, telling him to guess who had hit him. The Urantia Book says that this hour of humiliation was the bitterest part of his cup. Before this scene, today’s passage raises a searching question about human nature.

The passage asks, “⟦Q 184:4.5⟧What is this trait of the animal in man which leads him to want to insult and physically assault that which he cannot spiritually attain or intellectually achieve?⟦/Q⟧” And it diagnoses: “⟦Q 184:4.5⟧In the half-civilized man there still lurks an evil brutality which seeks to vent itself upon those who are superior in wisdom and spiritual attainment.⟦/Q⟧” This is an uncomfortable but honest observation. Faced with a goodness they cannot reach, people sometimes try to drag it down rather than be humbled by it. Because light exposes darkness, darkness hates the light.

This diagnosis does not apply only to the servants of that night. The same tendency lurks within us. When someone’s excellence or purity makes us feel small, we want to belittle that person, find fault, and mock. Envy and jealousy, gossip and cynicism, are this animal trait appearing in civilized dress. The Urantia Book teaches that man has evolved from animal origins, and that spiritual growth is the process of rising above these animal tendencies into a character worthy of the children of God (see Paper 103). Recognizing that impulse is the first step in overcoming it.

The last two sentences of the passage show a truth that shines through all this darkness. As the insults, taunts, and blows fell upon him, Jesus “⟦Q 184:4.5⟧was undefending but not defenseless.⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 184:4.5⟧Jesus was not vanquished, merely uncontending in the material sense.⟦/Q⟧” The Master did not remain still because he lacked the power to resist. As sovereign of the universe he could have saved himself at any moment, but in keeping with the Father’s will he chose not to use that power. His silence was not defeat but victory. And so this question must be turned toward ourselves before it is turned toward others.

The Master’s soul was rooted so deeply in the Father that no insult could wound it. The hands that struck him could reach his body, but they could not reach his peace and his love. This is the true meaning of nonresistance. Nonresistance is not weakness but a deeper strength that will not allow evil to rule us. When we do not repay evil with evil, we are not dragged along by the logic of evil but rise above it. True strength lies not in overcoming others but in mastering oneself.

If someone speaks to you unjustly or mocks you today, the urge to retaliate at once will arise. In that moment, remember the Master’s night. Remember that not striking back is not losing, and that a soul rooted in God is never vanquished. At the same time, look honestly within to see whether there is an animal impulse in you to belittle others. Pray that the quiet strength the Master showed may grow in us as well.
d347.pr: If you feel the urge to belittle someone today, find one good thing about that person and say it instead.

d348.t: The King Who Bears Witness to Truth
msg: Early on Friday morning Jesus stood before Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor. The Jewish leaders accused him of stirring up the people, of forbidding them to pay tribute to Caesar, and of claiming to be king of the Jews. Pilate took Jesus and John Zebedee aside into a room and questioned him. In particular he asked about the third charge, the claim to be a king. Today’s passage is the Master’s answer to that question. The examination looked like a political trial, but in truth it was the place where two kingdoms stood face to face.

Jesus asks Pilate, “⟦Q 185:3.3⟧Do you not perceive that my kingdom is not of this world?⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 185:3.3⟧If my kingdom were of this world, surely would my disciples fight that I should not be delivered into the hands of the Jews.⟦/Q⟧” The Master declares that his very presence there in bonds is proof that his kingdom is spiritual. The kings of the world defend their realms with armies and force, but the kingdom of Jesus is neither founded nor defended by the sword. His kingdom is built in the hearts of men. To the very end the Master was a king who ruled not by force but by love and truth.

The Master defines that kingdom as “⟦Q 185:3.3⟧the brotherhood of men who, through faith and by love, have become the sons of God.⟦/Q⟧” The whole heart of the gospel is contained in this brief definition. The way into the kingdom is not lineage or law but faith; the bond that holds the kingdom together is love; its citizens are all sons and daughters of God; and they are brothers and sisters to one another. And the Master adds that “⟦Q 185:3.3⟧this salvation is for the gentile as well as for the Jew.⟦/Q⟧” Spoken before Pilate, a Roman, these words were an open invitation to him as well.

When Pilate asked, “⟦Q 185:3.4⟧Then you are a king after all?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus answered, “⟦Q 185:3.4⟧Yes, I am such a king, and my kingdom is the family of the faith sons of my Father who is in heaven.⟦/Q⟧” Then he declared the purpose for which he was born into this world: “⟦Q 185:3.4⟧that I should show my Father to all men and bear witness to the truth of God.⟦/Q⟧” The Urantia Book teaches that Michael’s bestowal was above all to reveal the Universal Father (see Paper 120). Even in a courtroom where his life was at stake, Jesus bore witness to the Father rather than defend himself. His answer was not a plea to save himself but a testimony faithful to his mission to the end.

The Master’s final words were that “⟦Q 185:3.4⟧every one who loves the truth hears my voice.⟦/Q⟧” Pilate retorted, “⟦Q 185:3.5⟧What is truth?⟦/Q⟧” but never heard that voice. He stood before the truth, yet fear and political calculation kept him from following it. Knowing the truth and loving the truth are different things. Those who love the truth follow it even when it costs them. A heart that loves the truth grows together with the courage to bear the cost.

Of which kingdom are we living as citizens today? Are we following the world’s logic of power and success while calling Jesus king only with our lips? As citizens of the brotherhood bound together by faith and love, treat those you meet today as children of the same Father. And with a heart that loves the truth, listen for the Master’s voice. That voice still speaks within us today through the Spirit of Truth.
d348.pr: Among your choices today, settle on one decision you will make by the logic of the kingdom of God rather than the logic of the world.

msg: Though Pilate knew Jesus was innocent, he yielded to the pressure of the crowd and had him flogged. Then, when the Jewish leaders cried out that Jesus had claimed to be the Son of God, Pilate was seized with superstitious fear and called Jesus inside again for a last interview. Today’s passage is the scene of that final interview. It describes Pilate as “⟦Q 185:7.2⟧a man-fearing, weak, and vacillating judge.⟦/Q⟧” He was so unjust as to order a flogging before any proper sentence, even after declaring that he found no crime in him. He held power, but he lacked the courage to use it rightly.

Before such a Pilate, “⟦Q 185:7.2⟧Jesus looked Pilate straight in the face, but he did not answer him.⟦/Q⟧” The Master’s silence was not the silence of fear or resignation. He had already spoken the truth, and he knew that further words would not change Pilate’s decision. At times silence becomes a stronger testimony than words. Unable to bear that silence, Pilate pressed him: “⟦Q 185:7.2⟧Do you not realize that I still have power to release you or to crucify you?⟦/Q⟧”

Jesus’ answer is majestic: “⟦Q 185:7.2⟧You could have no power over me except it were permitted from above. You could exercise no authority over the Son of Man unless the Father in heaven allowed it.⟦/Q⟧” Pilate thought he decided everything, but in reality he was a man tossed about by his own fears and by the shouts of the crowd. The bound Jesus, on the other hand, was perfectly free within the Father’s will. True power depends not on who holds the sword but on who stands within the will of God. One who is gripped by fear is a slave even while holding power; one who trusts God is free even in chains.

Then Jesus showed astonishing mercy: “⟦Q 185:7.2⟧But you are not so guilty since you are ignorant of the gospel.⟦/Q⟧” Even toward the judge who had unjustly had him flogged, the Master was fair and took his ignorance into account. And he said, “⟦Q 185:7.2⟧He who betrayed me and he who delivered me to you, they have the greater sin.⟦/Q⟧” The Urantia Book teaches that God judges each person according to the light and understanding he has received. The one who knows more bears the greater responsibility. Even in the midst of his suffering, the Master never ceased to deal fairly with others.

This teaching gives us two lessons today. The first is not to fear the powers of the world. The people or circumstances that seem to grip and shake our lives are, in the end, under the sovereignty of God. No power in the world can truly harm a soul that stands in God. The second is to guard against Pilate’s weakness: fearing people, knowing what is right, and yet failing to do it. When we know the truth and stay silent or compromise, we too become the Pilate of that day.

If you are putting off doing what is right today because of someone’s pressure or opinion, remember the Master’s words. Nothing can truly harm me unless it is permitted from above. And when you exercise the small authority given to you over others, do not forget that you too are a steward of what has been given from above. When we carry out that stewardship with justice and mercy, we grow to resemble not Pilate but the Master.
d349.pr: Choose one right thing you have been putting off for fear of what others think, and find the courage to do it today.

d350.t: Man, Not God, Raised the Cross
msg: Looking upon the death of Jesus, many have long believed that it was a price fixed in heaven beforehand. But today’s passage quietly corrects this ancient idea: “⟦Q 186:5.2⟧It was man and not God who planned and executed the death of Jesus on the cross.⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 186:5.2⟧The Father in Paradise did not decree, demand, or require the death of his Son.⟦/Q⟧” All the Father did was refuse “⟦Q 186:5.2⟧to interfere with the march of human events on Urantia.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus would sooner or later have had to lay aside his mortal body, but “⟦Q 186:5.2⟧he could have executed such a task in countless ways without dying on a cross between two thieves.⟦/Q⟧”

This teaching is deeply bound up with what kind of God we know. The same section of Paper 186 says that the gospel of the good news, the truth that mortal man may by faith become conscious of being a son of God, is not dependent on the death of Jesus. The Father in heaven loved men just as much before Jesus came as he does now. A loving Father is not one who opens his heart only after blood has been shed, and Paper 188 emphasizes this again and again. The cross was not an offering to appease the wrath of God; it was the event in which human beings, gripped by ignorance, fear, and jealousy, rejected the light.

Why, then, did the Father not prevent it? The Universal Father respects the free will of his creatures, and he wished the bestowal Son to follow the natural course of human events like any ordinary mortal. Jesus himself chose not to save himself by supernatural power. Within that choice we see something astonishing. In the very midst of the darkest deed man ever committed, the Son of God did not lose his love and forgiveness, and he showed the whole universe that human evil can never overcome divine love.

Paper 186 also states plainly that Jesus did not die as a sacrifice for sin, nor to atone for the inborn moral guilt of the human race. Mankind bears no such racial guilt before God. Sin is chosen by the individual will, and its remedy likewise lies in the individual’s returning to the Father by faith. What we should feel before the cross, then, is not a vague sense of guilt but awe and gratitude for a divine love that embraced even the evil of men. This realization carries us from a religion of fear to a religion of love.

This truth also casts an important light on our daily lives. We often ask, in the face of the suffering or injustice that befalls us, whether God willed it. But much suffering comes from human ignorance and selfishness, and from the course of nature. God is not the one who contrived it but the one who walks with us through it and helps us turn it into material for spiritual growth. The indwelling Thought Adjuster is not the cause of our suffering but our guide beyond it.

Today, then, we can take two things to heart. First, we can lay down the old picture of God as one who punishes and exacts payment, and see him anew as the ever-loving Father. Second, if it was man who raised the cross, then raising up the way of love today is also our task as human beings. As hatred and fear made the cross, so faith and love build the brotherhood. May this be a day of watching carefully which of the two each of our small choices is building.
d350.pr: Call to mind one difficulty you are facing today, and quietly ask what God wishes to accomplish with you in the midst of it.

msg: The hours on the cross were hours of the most extreme suffering a human being can endure. Yet even then, “⟦Q 187:4.2⟧the Master had time amidst the pangs of mortal death to listen to the faith confession of the believing brigand.⟦/Q⟧” When the young brigand hanging beside him “⟦Q 187:4.2⟧reached out for salvation, he found deliverance.⟦/Q⟧” The passage says that “⟦Q 187:4.2⟧many times before this he had been constrained to believe in Jesus, but only in these last hours of consciousness did he turn with a whole heart toward the Master’s teaching.⟦/Q⟧” And what finally moved him was neither a miracle nor an argument but “⟦Q 187:4.2⟧the manner in which Jesus faced death.⟦/Q⟧”

This scene shows how wide the door of the kingdom of heaven stands open. Paper 187 adds that had any other of the jeering throng experienced the birth of faith within his soul and appealed to the mercy of Jesus, he too would have been received in the same way. Salvation is not a reward for merit accumulated but a gift received by faith. Even one who has been lost all his life enters into the reality of sonship if at the last moment he turns to the Father with a sincere heart. With the mercy of God there is no such thing as too late.

This story also teaches us that life itself is the most powerful sermon. The brigand had heard Jesus’ words before, but words alone had not fully opened his heart. When he saw Jesus, amid insult and agony, refuse to complain and ask forgiveness for those who crucified him, he could resist no longer. The conviction “⟦Q 187:4.2⟧that this Son of Man was indeed the Son of God⟦/Q⟧” came to him through such a living example. Truth moves people more deeply when it is shown in a life than when it is proved by logic.

Around us, too, are people who have come to the very threshold many times and turned away. Perhaps we ourselves are such people. There is no need to judge them or give up on them. God is patient, and the Spirit of Truth speaks to the human heart until the very last moment. Our task is not to win arguments but to reflect the Father by lives that keep faith and love even in hard moments. How we receive hardship may become, for someone, the last door that opens toward God.

Another lesson from this brigand’s conversion is that faith is never something we produce by our own strength alone. The passage says he had been “constrained” to believe many times. What drew him was a spiritual influence working ceaselessly within his mind. The Thought Adjuster who indwells us likewise draws us toward the Father, quietly yet persistently. Even when we are unaware of it, that drawing never stops. So the decision of faith is both our own choice and a response to the love of God that has long been waiting. If today, in some corner of your heart, you hear a longing for something higher, do not put it off; take hold of it now.

One more thing to take to heart is that the Master valued the salvation of one soul above his own suffering. When things are hard, we easily withdraw into ourselves. But even in his hardest moment, Jesus kept his heart open to others. Today, when we too are weighed down by our own burdens, let us listen for the small cry of someone beside us. In that listening we too will learn the heart of the Master.
d351.pr: When a hard moment comes today, respond with trust instead of complaint, and let your life reflect the Father to someone.

msg: “⟦Q 187:5.6⟧Jesus died royally — as he had lived.⟦/Q⟧” Today’s passage does not portray the day of the cross merely as a day of tragedy but as the day of a personality who “⟦Q 187:5.6⟧remained master of the situation throughout.⟦/Q⟧” Before his arrest he provided for the safety of his apostles, restrained Peter’s sword, and arranged for John to be near him to the end. Before the Sanhedrin he revealed his true nature, and he reminded Pilate of the source of his authority. And at last he “⟦Q 187:5.6⟧finished up his loving bestowal by handing over his spirit⟦/Q⟧” to the Paradise Father.

What stands out most in this portrait is that Jesus remained free to the very end. Soldiers led him away, yet he was not a victim being dragged off but a man walking a path he himself had chosen. As the opening of Paper 187 says, his submission to death on the cross was of his own free will. However much outward circumstances bound him, no one could take away an inner life that had committed itself to the Father’s will. True kingship lies not in outward power but in such an unshakable inner sovereignty.

The passage also shows that life and death are woven together as one. The composure, forgiveness, and thoughtfulness Jesus showed on the cross did not spring up suddenly that day. From his days as the carpenter of Nazareth, from his years as the eldest son caring for his family, and through the countless days of his public ministry, a life of choosing the Father’s will day by day came naturally to light in that final moment. People generally die as they have lived. What shows in a moment of crisis is the fruit of the choices we have made all along.

So the words “⟦Q 187:5.6⟧It is finished⟦/Q⟧” do not merely mean that the suffering was over; they are the confession of a life entrusted to him and lived out in full. We too hope to be able to say the same at the end of our lives. For that, we cannot neglect today. Not grand achievements but small choices, doing faithfully the work entrusted to us today, caring for those beside us, keeping our dignity even in the face of injustice, accumulate and prepare our last day.

Another thing to notice in the Master’s last hours is that even in his own suffering he kept caring for others to the end. He entrusted his mother to John, gave hope to the repentant brigand, and asked the Father’s forgiveness for those who crucified him. A royal death is not only a dignified bearing but a loving service that never stops, even to the last moment. Paper 188 says that what matters in Jesus’ death is not the fact of death but the noble spirit with which he met it. For us too, what we hold on to when life weighs heaviest reveals who we are. A heart that does not shut itself up in self-pity but stays open to others to the end: that is the true kingship the Master showed us.

Looking back over today, let us ask: if I were to end my life living just as I live now, could I say in peace, “⟦Q 187:5.6⟧It is finished⟦/Q⟧”? If we hesitate, that is no reason for despair but a reason to live anew from today. The indwelling Thought Adjuster leads us day by day to make choices a little closer to the Father’s will. As we live that way, we too, like the Master, will become people who stand as masters of our inner life in every situation.
d352.pr: Find one task you have put off or one relationship not yet reconciled, and take even a small step toward completing it today.

d353.t: The Cross, a Symbol of Service
msg: The cross is the most widely known symbol in Christian history, yet its meaning has long been interpreted in many ways. Today’s passage makes clear what the cross is not, and what it is. The cross “⟦Q 188:5.9⟧is not the symbol of the sacrifice of the innocent Son of God in the place of guilty sinners and in order to appease the wrath of an offended God.⟦/Q⟧” Rather, it is “⟦Q 188:5.9⟧that high symbol of sacred service, the devotion of one’s life to the welfare and salvation of one’s fellows.⟦/Q⟧” The cross is the picture of “⟦Q 188:5.9⟧the good bestowing themselves upon the evil and thereby saving them by this very devotion of love.⟦/Q⟧”

This teaching is in step with the whole current of Paper 188. In the preceding section the revelator says that the ideas of ransom and atonement are incompatible with the concept of the loving Father whom Jesus taught. God is not one who forgives only after receiving payment. The value of the cross, therefore, lies not in changing God’s mind but in changing the minds of men. The cross shows that Jesus’ attitude toward sinners was neither condemnation nor condonation but eternal and loving salvation.

The last sentence of the passage knocks especially at our hearts: “⟦Q 188:5.9⟧the very sight of this great symbol of the bestowal life of Jesus truly inspires all of us to want to go and do likewise.⟦/Q⟧” The cross is not merely an object to admire and venerate but an invitation to live in the same way. For more than twenty-five years Jesus bore the cross of mortal existence, and at the end he gave even his life. As we gaze upon that life, a longing for unselfish service awakens within us as well.

To take up the cross in daily life does not mean only grand martyrdom. Caring to the end for someone who shows no gratitude, praying for one who has hurt us, keeping our honesty even at a loss, setting aside a little of our own comfort to help carry another’s burden: all of these are the way of the cross. That way may look heavy, but service that springs from love in the end frees and enlarges our souls.

Paper 188 also says that Jesus’ suffering was not confined to the crucifixion. For long years he bore the cross of a real and intense mortal existence. The cross, then, is not the event of a single day but the crystallization of a lifetime of devotion. This is a great comfort to us. For the ordinary toil we bear each day, the sacrifices we make for our families, and our faithfulness in unseen places are all linked to that great symbol. Even service no one notices, the Father sees in full. And when we remember that countless creatures across the universe, tempted to give up the struggle of faith, have taken fresh strength from gazing upon this cross, we know that our own small devotion is never in vain.

When you look upon the cross today, may you look not with fear or guilt but with gratitude and resolve. God did not give up his Son in order to punish us; he showed us how far love can go. Having received that love, we can now become channels through which it flows. When we give ourselves for one another, the cross is no longer an event of the past but a living sign in our lives today.
d353.pr: Today, quietly give your time or effort to someone without expecting anything in return.

msg: In the midst of the record of the resurrection, the revelator pauses to put a profound question to us. “⟦Q 189:1.3⟧Mankind is slow to perceive that, in all that is personal, matter is the skeleton of morontia, and that both are the reflected shadow of enduring spirit reality.⟦/Q⟧” And he asks: “⟦Q 189:1.3⟧How long before you will regard time as the moving image of eternity and space as the fleeting shadow of Paradise realities?⟦/Q⟧” This brief paragraph is a key to understanding the resurrection and an invitation to change the way we look at the world.

In Jesus’ resurrection his material body remained in the tomb. What rose was not the flesh but the personality, and he came forth in a morontia form, just as ascending mortals awaken on the mansion worlds (see Paper 189, section 1). The material body was a temporary vessel for what is eternal, and the personality and spirit identity that grew within it were what truly endured. Many of the things we cling to, our bodies and possessions, our status and visible achievements, are in the end shadows reflecting a deeper reality.

This does not mean we should take the material world lightly. Just as a body cannot stand without a skeleton, material experience is an essential foundation for the growth of the soul. We are simply not to mistake the shadow for the reality. The failures and losses we suffer today loom large, but they are only one scene in the long film of eternity. Conversely, the small choices of love and the decisions for truth we make today, however fleeting they may seem, are inscribed in eternal reality.

To regard time as the moving image of eternity is to know that this present moment is not cut off from eternity. The indwelling Thought Adjuster is transcribing the experiences of time in our minds into eternal values. And so our days are not merely time flowing past but the very stuff of reality the soul gathers as it advances toward the morontia and spirit levels. When we hold this perspective, impatience and anxiety diminish and a serene trust takes their place.

This truth also changes the way we look at people. The person before us is not merely a being made up of a body, an appearance, and a social role. Within is a soul growing toward eternity, and indwelling is the Thought Adjuster, the spirit of the Universal Father. Outward appearances change and pass away with time, but the spiritual reality growing within that person endures forever. Remembering this, we will no longer judge people rashly or treat them lightly. Even before the aged and the sick, even before those who have failed, we can see the eternal possibility dwelling within them. Just as the risen Jesus left his body in the tomb and came forth as a morontia personality, all of us will one day cast off the shadows and meet one another in truer form. Honoring one another today, with our eyes on that day, is practice in living eternity.

Today, when something weighs on your heart, pause and ask: Is this shadow or reality? Seen with the eyes of eternity, how much does this matter? And within it, look for and hold fast to what will endure forever: love, truth, and goodness. As we do so, we too, little by little, like the risen Master, will become people who awaken beyond matter toward eternal reality.
d354.pr: Choose one worry that is capturing your heart today, and write down how much it matters when seen with the eyes of eternity.

msg: When the risen Jesus came forth from the tomb, it did not end as a special miracle that happened to one person alone. Today’s passage says that the power inherent in Jesus, “⟦Q 190:0.2⟧the endowment of life,⟦/Q⟧” which enabled him to rise from the dead, “⟦Q 190:0.2⟧is the very gift of eternal life which he bestows upon kingdom believers.⟦/Q⟧” And this gift “⟦Q 190:0.2⟧even now makes certain their resurrection from the bonds of natural death.⟦/Q⟧” The revelator goes on to tell us that “⟦Q 190:0.3⟧the mortals of the realms will arise in the morning of the resurrection with the same type of transition or morontia body that Jesus had when he arose from the tomb on this Sunday morning.⟦/Q⟧”

This teaching changes our thinking about death at its very root. The resurrection of Jesus showed us in advance the path we are to walk. He chose to experience in person the morontia career through which ascending mortals pass (see the opening of Paper 190), and through that experience he showed that life beyond death is not a vague hope but a real next stage. “⟦Q 190:0.3⟧These bodies do not have circulating blood, and such beings do not partake of ordinary material food; nevertheless, these morontia forms are real.⟦/Q⟧” Those who saw the risen Master were not deceived; “⟦Q 190:0.3⟧they really saw him.⟦/Q⟧”

How, then, does this promise become ours? Eternal life is a gift received by faith. When we truly believe the Father and choose to do his will, an eternal soul grows together with the indwelling Thought Adjuster. When death comes, that soul does not vanish; it awakens in new form on the mansion worlds and continues the journey of ascension. The hope of resurrection, therefore, is not a tale of the distant future but is bound up with the decisions of faith we make today.

Those who believe this truth deeply are not seized by fear in the face of death. The grief of parting from a loved one is still real, but that grief rests not in despair but in the hope of meeting again. We can also grow calm in the face of our own frailty and aging, for though the body declines, the soul can be renewed day by day. It was this very faith in the resurrection that kept the early believers from losing their joy even under persecution.

Paper 190 says that unwavering faith in the resurrection was central to every branch of the early gospel teaching. In Jerusalem, in Alexandria, and in Antioch, believers stood on this hope. Yet we must remember that the heart of resurrection faith is not the fact of the empty tomb itself but the encounter with the living Master (see Paper 189, section 2). Mary Magdalene, Peter, and the two brothers on the road to Emmaus were all transformed when they met the living Lord. Our resurrection faith, too, gains its power only when it goes beyond assent to doctrine and leads into personal communion with the spirit living and working within us today. In that communion, eternal life begins not in some distant future but already now.

May we too become people who live the resurrection morning in advance. That means not waiting vaguely for what comes after death but living a life invested in eternal values here and now. Each day of loving, forgiving, following the truth, and seeking the Father’s will is time spent preparing for the morontia career. Remembering that the very life by which Jesus rose from the tomb has already been given to us as a gift, let us walk through today in hope instead of fear.
d355.pr: Call to mind one fear of death or loss, and meditate on how the promise of resurrection transforms that fear.

msg: The risen Jesus appeared to the apostles and believers on their way to Galilee and declared once more what kind of kingdom he had come to establish. “⟦Q 191:6.2⟧That which my Father sent me into the world to establish belongs not to a race, a nation, nor to a special group of teachers or preachers.⟦/Q⟧” It “⟦Q 191:6.2⟧belongs to both Jew and gentile, to rich and poor, to free and bond, to male and female, even to the little children.⟦/Q⟧” This declaration shows that from the very beginning the gospel was universal news that crosses every wall.

These words echo again and again through the post-resurrection appearances recorded in Paper 191. To the believers at Philadelphia and to the apostles in the upper chamber alike, the Master spoke of one Father in heaven and one gospel. And he added that this gospel would not be left in the mere keeping of priests (see Paper 191, section 6). The truth of the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of men can never become the possession of any particular institution or class. Every person who believes it is both an heir and a bearer of this gospel. After Pentecost this gospel did in fact spread beyond the boundaries of nation and language, and Paper 194 says that on that day the religion of Jesus broke through all national restrictions and racial fetters. The words the Master spoke on the hills of Galilee were not merely an ideal but a promise soon to be fulfilled in history. And that promise continues to be fulfilled today through our lives.

How, then, is this gospel to be proclaimed? The Master said to proclaim it not by words alone but “⟦Q 191:6.2⟧by the lives which you live in the flesh.⟦/Q⟧” And he told them exactly how: “⟦Q 191:6.2⟧You shall love one another with a new and startling affection, even as I have loved you. You will serve mankind with a new and amazing devotion, even as I have served you.⟦/Q⟧” The most powerful evidence for the gospel is not a logical explanation but the lives of people transformed by love and service.

The last part of the passage is especially beautiful. “⟦Q 191:6.2⟧When men see you so love them, and when they behold how fervently you serve them, they will perceive that you have become faith-fellows of the kingdom of heaven, and they will follow after the Spirit of Truth which they see in your lives, to the finding of eternal salvation.⟦/Q⟧” This means our lives can become windows through which the Spirit of Truth shines for others. It is a great honor and at the same time a weighty responsibility. People meet God through the way we live more than through what we say.

Even today we live, knowingly or not, building walls. Nationality and race, wealth and education, religious affiliation and political leaning often become the lines that divide people. But before the gospel of Jesus all these distinctions become secondary. All people are children of the same Universal Father, and the spirit of the Father indwells them all. When we sincerely accept this fact, even those we thought of as strangers, even those we found uncomfortable, begin to appear as brothers and sisters.

Today, look honestly at whom you have been keeping, in your heart, outside the gospel. Then offer that person a small kindness and respect. It need not be grand evangelism. Loving as the Master loved us and serving as he served us, in these small acts, is the gospel we proclaim today. As we do so, the kingdom will quietly widen from one heart to another.
d356.pr: Today, offer one warm word to someone you have kept at a distance, treating them as the Master has treated you.

msg: After breakfast by the Sea of Galilee, the risen Master walked along the shore with Peter and asked, “⟦Q 192:2.2⟧Peter, do you love me?⟦/Q⟧” When Peter answered, “⟦Q 192:2.2⟧Lord, you know I love you with all my soul,⟦/Q⟧” the Master did not let that confession of love rest in feeling but turned it at once into a concrete commission: “⟦Q 192:2.2⟧If you love me, Peter, feed my lambs.⟦/Q⟧” He was to minister to the weak, the poor, and the young, to preach the gospel “⟦Q 192:2.2⟧without fear or favor,⟦/Q⟧” and to serve and forgive even as the Master had served and forgiven him.

To feel the weight of this scene, we must remember that only days before, Peter had denied his Master three times. The Peter who had warmed himself by the charcoal fire in the courtyard of Annas that night now faced the Master again beside a charcoal fire on the lakeshore. The Master did not rebuke him for his failure. Instead, he asked about love and entrusted him with a mission (see Paper 192, section 2). God’s forgiveness does not dig up the past in order to punish; it raises up the one who has fallen and entrusts him with new work. To the Peter who had denied him three times, the Master three times asked about love and three times gave a charge. Through that repetition Peter’s wounds were healed one by one. The Master knew that trust changes a person more deeply than reproach. And after Pentecost, Peter did indeed become a leader who boldly proclaimed the gospel.

The Master’s charge to Peter shows concretely what love is. To love the Master is not a surge of religious feeling but the care of those whom he loved. It means turning our hearts especially toward the weak, the poor, and the young, those with little strength to protect themselves. Since “⟦Q 192:2.2⟧God is no respecter of persons,⟦/Q⟧” neither should we measure our care by a person’s status or usefulness.

The passage’s final charge is striking: “⟦Q 192:2.2⟧Let experience teach you the value of meditation and the power of intelligent reflection.⟦/Q⟧” For the hasty and impulsive Peter, this was a much-needed teaching. Service cannot long endure on zeal alone. Love becomes wise only when there is time to stop quietly, commune with the Father, and learn by reflecting on one’s experience. Meditation is not an escape from service but the wellspring that makes service deep and healthy.

Like Peter, we confess our love for the Master and yet stumble in actual life. At such times we easily sink into self-reproach and think ourselves useless. But the Master asks us the same question today: “⟦Q 192:2.2⟧Do you love me?⟦/Q⟧” And if our answer is sincere, he entrusts us with our mission again, regardless of our past failures. A fall need not be an end; it can be the starting point for learning a humbler and deeper love.

Who are the lambs around us today? They may be a lonely elderly person, a weary coworker, a child with a wounded heart, or a neighbor in need. Let us express our love for the Master in small acts of care toward them. And at the end of the day, let us take a moment for meditation and ask the Father what today’s experiences have taught us. When the confession of love, the practice of service, and quiet reflection come together, we will grow, like Peter, into shepherds more and more like the Master.
d357.pr: Find one person around you who needs care today, and express your love for the Master in a small act of service.

msg: Jesus’ farewell message to the apostles included a reference to the loss of Judas and a solemn warning against the dangers of social and fraternal isolation. Looking back on that tragedy, today’s passage points to the chief reason Judas went wrong: “⟦Q 193:4.2⟧he was very markedly an isolated personality.⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 193:4.2⟧He persistently refused to confide in, or freely fraternize with, his fellow apostles.⟦/Q⟧” And he nursed within himself such psychologic enemies as grudges and revenge.

But the passage adds a very important qualification: “⟦Q 193:4.2⟧his being an isolated type of personality would not, in and of itself, have wrought such mischief for Judas.⟦/Q⟧” The problem was that “⟦Q 193:4.2⟧he also failed to increase in love and grow in spiritual grace.⟦/Q⟧” A reserved temperament is not in itself a fault. Quiet people too can love deeply and grow greatly. But when we close the door of the heart and refuse the exchange of love, we become shut up in our own hurts and disappointments and grow ever darker.

Paper 193 lists the weaknesses of Judas in several ways. He never learned to accept disappointment as a common feature of human existence, he disliked facing facts frankly, and he was reluctant to discuss his problems with his closest friends (see Paper 193, section 4). In the end he ignored those who loved him in life, and in death he was friendless. Though he had the best of companions beside him, Jesus and his eleven fellows, he was alone to the very last. As Paper 193 says, his isolation doubled his grief, multiplied his sorrow, augmented his anxiety, and made his despair almost unbearable. A burden carried alone feels far heavier than it really is. Had he shared the same disappointment with those who loved him, its weight would have been much lighter. Peter too suffered a great failure, but because he came back to his companions and opened his heart, he was able to rise again.

This story does not end as merely the tale of a betrayer of long ago. Every one of us, when we suffer disappointment and hurt, is tempted to close our hearts. Feeling that no one understands us, we easily isolate ourselves and brood over our grievances. Resentment piled up in this way clouds our judgment and in the end makes even those who love us look like enemies. The tragedy of Judas was not the decision of a moment but the result of a heart long kept closed.

The kingdom Jesus taught is a brotherhood. We were not made to walk the path of faith alone. The soul grows healthy within relationships in which we open our hearts to one another, share our burdens, seek counsel, and give and receive forgiveness. The indwelling Thought Adjuster draws us toward God and at the same time toward our brothers and sisters. If we say we love God while walling ourselves off from people, something in that faith has grown sick.

Today, look honestly to see whether there is a disappointment or resentment you are carrying alone. Then gently bring it out before a trusted friend or family member. Opening the heart takes courage, but it is that very courage that rescues us from the darkness of isolation. When we do not hide our disappointments but share them in love, they do not harden into grudges but become instead the soil of growth. For one who grows in love, isolation is no longer a danger.
d358.pr: Today, share honestly with someone you trust one disappointment or worry you have been carrying alone.

d359.t: Where the Spirit’s Proof Is Found
msg: When the Spirit of Truth was poured out at Pentecost, the believers experienced great joy and power. But today’s passage corrects a common misunderstanding about this spirit: “⟦Q 194:2.4⟧Do not make the mistake of expecting to become strongly intellectually conscious of the outpoured Spirit of Truth.⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 194:2.4⟧The spirit never creates a consciousness of himself, only a consciousness of Michael, the Son.⟦/Q⟧” Therefore “⟦Q 194:2.4⟧the proof … of your fellowship with the Spirit of Truth is not to be found in your consciousness of this spirit but rather in your experience of enhanced fellowship with Michael.⟦/Q⟧”

“⟦Q 194:2.4⟧From the beginning Jesus taught that the spirit would not speak of himself.⟦/Q⟧” The Spirit of Truth is like light. We do not see light itself; we see the things it illuminates. In the same way, the Spirit of Truth does not reveal himself but reveals Jesus. The spirit’s working shows itself as we come to understand Jesus’ life more deeply, as his teachings come to us more vividly, and as our desire to be like him grows stronger. So there is no need to anxiously search our inner life without end to confirm the spirit’s presence. Rather, when we fix our gaze on Jesus and look upon his life, the spirit is already at work in that very looking. This humble way of the Spirit of Truth shows that the spirits of God do not put themselves forward but delight only in revealing the Father and the Son.

Paper 194 says that the first mission of the Spirit of Truth is to foster and personalize truth, for the comprehension of truth constitutes the highest form of human liberty. The spirit also helps believers remember and understand the Master’s words and illuminates his life on earth (see Paper 194, section 2). Since the coming of the Spirit of Truth, man has received a threefold guidance: the Thought Adjuster, the spirit of the Father; the Spirit of Truth, the spirit of the Son; and the Holy Spirit, the spirit of the Universe Spirit.

This teaching tells us where to look for confirmation of our experience of faith. Some think the spirit is present only when there are special feelings or mysterious phenomena. So when such experiences are absent they grow anxious, and some go chasing after them. But the true fruits of the spirit are quiet. The way to confirm the spirit’s presence is to ask whether we forgive more readily than before, whether we love the truth more, and whether we trust more fully the Father whom Jesus revealed.

This is also a lesson in humility. Just as the Spirit of Truth reveals not himself but Jesus, one who lives by the spirit reveals the Master rather than himself. As faith deepens, we do not boast of our spirituality but instead long for others to see the Father’s love through us. If our attention is drawn to how spiritual we are, it may be a sign that not the spirit but the self is standing in front.

Today, rather than wandering in search of spiritual experiences, meditate deeply on a single scene from the life of Jesus. Recall how he treated people and how he trusted the Father, and ask that something of that likeness may grow within you. As our fellowship with Michael grows in this way, we will know, without straining to confirm it, that the Spirit of Truth is with us. The proof of the spirit is the Master’s face growing ever clearer in our lives.
d359.pr: Today, meditate on one scene from the life of Jesus, and put into practice one action that helps you become like him.

msg: Pentecost is easily remembered for the miracle of tongues or for astonishing phenomena, but Paper 194 states clearly what its true gift was. “⟦Q 194:3.12⟧Pentecost endowed mortal man with the power to forgive personal injuries, to keep sweet in the midst of the gravest injustice, to remain unmoved in the face of appalling danger, and to challenge the evils of hate and anger by the fearless acts of love and forbearance.⟦/Q⟧” The Spirit of Truth did not come to make people look special but to make them strong from within.

The passage then looks back over the history of war on Urantia. All participants in those great and destructive struggles met with defeat; “⟦Q 194:3.12⟧there was only one who came out of these embittered struggles with an enhanced reputation — that was Jesus of Nazareth and his gospel of overcoming evil with good.⟦/Q⟧” A victory won by force breeds further hatred and revenge, but a victory won by love turns enemies into brothers. That is why “⟦Q 194:3.12⟧the secret of a better civilization is bound up in the Master’s teachings of the brotherhood of man, the good will of love and mutual trust.⟦/Q⟧”

This teaching was shown most clearly in Jesus’ own life. Throughout the day of his trials and the cross, he did not retaliate against insult and violence, and he asked forgiveness for those who were killing him (see Paper 188, section 5). This was not weakness but the greatest strength. The spirit poured out at Pentecost is the very spirit of that Jesus. So those who receive the Spirit of Truth discover within themselves the strength Jesus showed, the power not to answer hatred with hatred. The apostles themselves were witnesses to this. They who had scattered in fear before the cross were fearless after Pentecost in the face of threats and persecution, and to those who hated them they proclaimed the gospel instead of hatred. Their transformation shows how wonderfully the power given by the spirit can change ordinary people.

Our daily lives are not great battlefields, but they are full of small skirmishes. Faced with rude words, unfair treatment, misunderstanding and blame, we reflexively want to fight back and repay. But when we do, our hearts too are stained with anger just like the other person’s. The power to forgive is not ignoring injustice; it is refusing to let injustice rule our souls. Keeping sweet is not servility but an inner freedom rooted in the Father’s will.

This power is not gained by our own willpower alone. As the words “gift of Pentecost” say, it is an endowment that comes from the spirit. Our part is to make room in our hearts to receive that gift. Prayer does not bring the spirit to us, but it enlarges our capacity to receive (see Paper 194, section 3). The habit of pausing when anger rises and turning our hearts to the indwelling spirit gradually shapes us into new people.

If someone offends or hurts you today, try to see that moment as an opportunity to test the power of Pentecost. Rather than reacting at once, take a breath, and remember that this person too is a child of the same Father. Then respond as gently as you can. As these small victories add up, the gospel of Jesus, overcoming evil with good, will quietly spread through our homes, our workplaces, and our society.
d360.pr: When a hurtful moment comes today, take one breath and answer with a gentle word instead of repaying in kind.

msg: In dealing with the challenge of the materialism that has swept the modern world, Paper 195 sets a word of deep comfort at its very center. “⟦Q 195:6.16⟧Freedom or initiative in any realm of existence is directly proportional to the degree of spiritual influence and cosmic-mind control; that is, in human experience, the degree of the actuality of doing ‘the Father’s will.’⟦/Q⟧” And it adds: “⟦Q 195:6.16⟧when you once start out to find God, that is the conclusive proof that God has already found you.⟦/Q⟧” It goes on to say that “⟦Q 195:6.17⟧the sincere pursuit of goodness, beauty, and truth leads to God.⟦/Q⟧”

Materialism sees man as a soulless machine and the universe as a purposeless mechanism (see Paper 195, section 6). In such a worldview, neither freedom nor meaning nor the longing for God can be explained. But the revelator tells us that the very fact that we seek truth and long for God is proof that we are more than machines. If the universe were only matter, a mind seeking something beyond matter could never have arisen within it. Paper 195 goes so far as to say that the very pessimism of the most pessimistic materialist is proof that the universe is not wholly material. A mind that seeks meaning, a mind that suffers over meaninglessness, reveals in itself that something beyond the machine dwells within us. Our questions and longings are not accidental nerve impulses but signs of a soul open toward eternity.

The words that the heart seeking God is proof that God has already found us change the starting point of our faith. We often think of faith as our first striving to draw near to God. In reality, the Thought Adjuster indwelling us was there first, and the longing in our hearts for something higher is an echo of his call. The very desire to seek God is already the Father’s touch.

The passage also speaks of scientific discovery. “⟦Q 195:6.17⟧The discoverer was free to make the discovery. The thing discovered is real and apparently uniform.⟦/Q⟧” That is, freedom and order exist together in the universe. A scientist seeking truth, an artist seeking beauty, an ordinary person trying to do good: all of these can become paths that lead to God. Truth, beauty, and goodness are values of Paradise, and those who sincerely pursue them are walking toward God, whether they know it or not.

These words are a great comfort to those in doubt and wandering. Those who suffer because they cannot be sure of God, and those who feel their faith has dried up, are already on the path if they are still seeking something. God is not one who meets us only after we have reached perfect certainty; he is with us even in the moment of our seeking. What matters, then, is not to stop seeking, and to keep an honest heart turned toward truth and goodness.

These words also remind us that freedom is proportional to the degree to which we do the Father’s will. We easily think that doing as we please is freedom, but true freedom grows as we live in harmony with spiritual reality. Today, let us follow one truth more honestly, savor one beauty more deeply, and practice one more good deed. In those small pursuits we will sense the footsteps of the Father who has already come looking for us.
d361.pr: Today, recognize the longing for goodness and truth stirring within you as God’s call reaching you first, and give thanks for it.

msg: “⟦Q 195:9.8⟧The world needs more firsthand religion.⟦/Q⟧” Today’s passage observes that even Christianity, “⟦Q 195:9.8⟧the best of the religions of the twentieth century,⟦/Q⟧” is “⟦Q 195:9.8⟧not only a religion about Jesus, but it is so largely one which men experience secondhand.⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 195:9.8⟧They take their religion wholly as handed down by their accepted religious teachers.⟦/Q⟧” But the revelator exclaims, almost with a sigh: “⟦Q 195:9.8⟧What an awakening the world would experience if it could only see Jesus as he really lived on earth and know, firsthand, his life-giving teachings!⟦/Q⟧”

Secondhand religion is a faith that hears about the God someone else experienced and accepts it. That too is precious as a beginning. We first learn faith through our parents, teachers, and communities. But if we stop there, religion never becomes our own; it remains like borrowed clothing. Paper 195 says that Christianity has changed from the religion of Jesus into a religion about Jesus (see Paper 195, section 4). Instead of believing together what Jesus believed, it has stopped at believing doctrines about Jesus. Paper 195 says that while primitive man lived in the bondage of superstitious religious fear, modern civilized man dreads the thought of falling under the dominance of strong religious convictions (see Paper 195, section 9). So people try to control living religion by rationalizing and institutionalizing it, and they hide behind other people’s faith to avoid a direct encounter with God. But firsthand religion is not bondage; it is liberation. Only those who know God firsthand can live freely, without fear.

The passage offers a beautiful comparison: “⟦Q 195:9.8⟧Descriptive words of things beautiful cannot thrill like the sight thereof, neither can creedal words inspire men’s souls like the experience of knowing the presence of God.⟦/Q⟧” However much we read a description of a sunset, it cannot replace the thrill of the moment we gaze upon the sunset itself. In the same way, even an accurate account of God cannot replace living communion with God.

How, then, is firsthand religion possible? The Urantia Book teaches that the Universal Father personally indwells each person as the Thought Adjuster. God is not far away, to be met only through intermediaries; he lives with us in the deepest place of our hearts. Anyone, therefore, can commune with God directly by faith and through sincere worship and prayer. This is the heart of the religion Jesus lived out in his own life.

The last sentence of the passage gives hope: “⟦Q 195:9.8⟧expectant faith will ever keep the hope-door of man’s soul open for the entrance of the eternal spiritual realities of the divine values of the worlds beyond.⟦/Q⟧” Even if you have not yet clearly experienced the presence of God, there is no need to be discouraged. A faith that waits with expectation and keeps the door open is itself already the road to firsthand religion. As long as the door stays open, eternal reality can enter at any time.

Today, seek not the God you have heard about from others but the God you meet yourself. Set aside a quiet time and speak to the Father with a sincere heart instead of formal words. And read the life of Jesus in the Gospels just as it is, without interpretation or doctrine. As we look directly at how he prayed, how he treated people, and how he trusted the Father, our faith will be transformed from something borrowed into living experience.
d362.pr: Today, take five minutes to speak honestly to the Father in your own words instead of a set prayer.

d363.t: What Is Needed Now Is Jesus
msg: The last section of Paper 195 acknowledges the contribution of Christianity while drawing a clear conclusion: “⟦Q 195:10.1⟧Christianity has indeed done a great service for this world, but what is now most needed is Jesus.⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 195:10.1⟧The world needs to see Jesus living again on earth in the experience of spirit-born mortals.⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 195:10.1⟧It is futile to talk about a revival of primitive Christianity,⟦/Q⟧” the revelator says; “⟦Q 195:10.1⟧you must go forward from where you find yourselves.⟦/Q⟧”

These words teach us not to idealize the past. The early church had zeal, but it also had many misunderstandings and compromises (see the opening of Paper 195). What we must recover is not the institutions or forms of a particular era but the life and teachings of Jesus himself. “⟦Q 195:10.1⟧Modern culture must become spiritually baptized with a new revelation of Jesus’ life and illuminated with a new understanding of his gospel of eternal salvation.⟦/Q⟧” This is also why the life of Jesus is recorded in such detail in the Urantia Book.

The passage says that “⟦Q 195:10.1⟧when Jesus becomes thus lifted up, he will draw all men to himself.⟦/Q⟧” What draws people is not the refinement of doctrine or the size of an organization but the beauty of the personality of Jesus. Elsewhere Paper 195 says that many earnest people would gladly give their loyalty to the Christ of the gospel, but are disappointed in a church that fails to reveal the meaning of his life and teachings (see Paper 195, section 10). People still long for Jesus. What they have turned away from is not Jesus but the forms and quarrels that hide him. Our task, therefore, is not to repackage Jesus but to clear away whatever hides him and reveal his life just as it was. When the road he walked and the way he loved are seen as they truly are, people’s hearts will turn to him naturally.

How, then, will Jesus live again on earth? Through the lives of those who follow him. The passage says that “⟦Q 195:10.1⟧Jesus’ disciples should be more than conquerors, even overflowing sources of inspiration and enhanced living to all men.⟦/Q⟧” A conqueror subdues others, but an overflowing source brings life to everything around it. When our faith is not used to win arguments but becomes a spring that waters other people’s lives, Jesus lives again within us.

The last sentence of the passage is sharp: “⟦Q 195:10.1⟧Religion is only an exalted humanism until it is made divine by the discovery of the reality of the presence of God in personal experience.⟦/Q⟧” Good ethics and social service are precious, but by themselves they are not yet religion. True religion begins in living communion with the indwelling spirit of the Father. Only when the love flowing from that communion becomes service does the religion of Jesus take root in our lives.

Today we may ask ourselves: can those who look at my life see Jesus in it? This question is not a burden but an invitation. When small moments gather, of trusting the Father as Jesus did, loving people as Jesus did, and serving willingly as Jesus did, the world will meet the living Jesus again. If what the world needs most now is Jesus, then the nearest place where we can show him is our own daily life today.
d363.pr: Today, live with one thing consciously in mind so that those who see your words and actions may glimpse Jesus in them.

msg: “⟦Q 196:0.13⟧Jesus does not require his disciples to believe in him but rather to believe with him.⟦/Q⟧” Today’s passage holds, briefly yet profoundly, the heart of the final paper, which deals with the faith of Jesus. The Master invites us to “⟦Q 196:0.13⟧believe in the reality of the love of God and in full confidence accept the security of the assurance of sonship with the heavenly Father.⟦/Q⟧” Not only “⟦Q 196:0.13⟧to believe what he believed, but also to believe as he believed⟦/Q⟧”: “⟦Q 196:0.13⟧this is the full significance of his one supreme requirement, ‘Follow me.’⟦/Q⟧”

This difference may seem small, but it completely changes the character of faith. Faith in Jesus places Jesus outside us and makes him its object. But faith with Jesus stands beside him and looks in the same direction he looks. That direction is the Father in Paradise. Paper 196 says that Jesus enjoyed a sublime and wholehearted faith in God (see the opening of Paper 196). We are called not merely to adore that faith but to share it. The life of Jesus was the doing of God’s will, the living of the human life religiously by faith. He does not ask us to watch that life but calls us to join in it. To follow him is not to mechanically imitate his footsteps but to receive into ourselves the spirit of the faith that moved him (see Paper 196, section 1).

Paper 196 also hopes that one day the reform of the Christian church may go deep enough to return to the pure religious teachings of Jesus, the author and finisher of our faith (see Paper 196, section 2). Believing in the divinity of Jesus is important, but it must not obscure the sharing of his human faith. Jesus is the most perfect example of one who, as a man like us, believed and trusted the Father. His faith is not something beyond our reach but a path we too can walk together with him.

What was the faith of Jesus like? It reached the purity of a child’s trust, and it never wavered before any crisis. He did not regard the universe as hostile, and he trusted the Father’s care completely. Yet his faith was never fanatical; it was practical and open toward his neighbors. To believe with him is to learn this trust and this balance in our own lives.

What does it mean to believe with Jesus in daily life? When worries come crowding in, it means recalling how Jesus would have trusted the Father. Before an uncertain future, it means leaning on the security that the assurance of sonship gives. Even when people disappoint us, it means not letting go of the faith that all people are children of the Father. When we do this, we no longer merely look up to Jesus from afar; we walk side by side with him and make his faith our own.

Today, picture the Master standing beside you, looking with you toward the Father. And hold together with him the simple and profound trust that he held. When difficulties arise, believe with him in the Father’s goodness; when joys come, give thanks to the Father with him. This is the truest way to answer the call “Follow me,” and the way our faith becomes living experience.
d364.pr: Take one thing that worries you today and believe together with Jesus, recalling how he would have trusted the Father.

msg: Near the very end of the Urantia Book, the revelator sums up the greatest challenge facing modern man: “⟦Q 196:3.34⟧to achieve better communication with the divine Monitor that dwells within the human mind.⟦/Q⟧” And he says that “⟦Q 196:3.34⟧man’s greatest adventure in the flesh consists in the well-balanced and sane effort to advance the borders of self-consciousness out through the dim realms of embryonic soul-consciousness in a wholehearted effort to reach the borderland of spirit-consciousness — contact with the divine presence.⟦/Q⟧”

The divine Monitor spoken of here is the Thought Adjuster who indwells us. The Universal Father has given each person a fragment of his own spirit, and that spirit works in our minds whether we are awake or asleep. The problem is not that he is far away but that we do not attend to communion with him. The challenge of this age is not a lack of technology or knowledge but the shallowness of our relationship with the one who already dwells within us. Every day we take in countless pieces of information and listen to countless voices, yet we scarcely listen to the quiet leading of the one who is nearest of all. The Thought Adjuster does not compel us; he waits. Each time we turn our hearts and choose to cooperate with him, that communion deepens a little, and our souls grow by that much.

The passage shows that this adventure proceeds in stages. We begin with self-consciousness, the level of being aware of ourselves as persons. Next we pass through the dim realm of embryonic soul-consciousness, where we sense moral values and spiritual meanings. And at last we reach spirit-consciousness, the experience of knowing the presence of God. This is not a leap made overnight but a journey of growth that continues throughout life and beyond.

It is also important that the revelator stresses a “⟦Q 196:3.34⟧well-balanced and sane effort.⟦/Q⟧” Turning our backs on reality or sinking into strange emotions in pursuit of spiritual experience is not the true adventure. Paper 196 says that the faith of Jesus was never fanatical. God-consciousness is not an escape from daily life but a deeper living of it. When communion with the divine presence grows in the midst of an ordinary life of working, loving, and serving, that is healthy spirituality.

The passage says that “⟦Q 196:3.34⟧such spirit-consciousness is the equivalent of the knowledge of the actuality of sonship with God.⟦/Q⟧” And it adds, “⟦Q 196:3.34⟧Otherwise, the assurance of sonship is the experience of faith.⟦/Q⟧” This is a great comfort. Even those who are not yet clearly conscious of God’s presence can be assured by faith that they are children of God. Faith is the bridge to spirit-consciousness, and even while we are crossing that bridge, we are already the Father’s children.

Today, let us take a small step in this greatest of adventures. Pause for a moment in your day, set aside the noise of the outer world, and turn your heart toward the divine Monitor within you. Rather than trying to gain something, simply rest in his presence. Then carry the peace you have found in that stillness back into your daily life and into your dealings with others. As these small communions are repeated day after day, we will grow, little by little, into people who know God.
d365.pr: Today, pause quietly for ten minutes and rest in the presence of the Thought Adjuster within you.
